author: Living With Arthritis Editorial Team

content:
Quick answer: Pregnancy with arthritis often goes well, but treatment and disease control need individual planning with your rheumatology and maternity teams. Some medicines are not suitable during pregnancy; never stop or change prescribed treatment without specialist advice.

Planning before pregnancy

Book a pre-pregnancy appointment with your rheumatology team. Discuss disease activity, other health conditions, current medicines, vaccinations and any previous pregnancy complications. The aim is to control inflammation with treatments that are appropriate for your circumstances.

Reviewing arthritis medicines

Methotrexate is not suitable during pregnancy and needs specialist planning before conception. Other medicines have different safety profiles and decisions may depend on the type of arthritis, dose, stage of pregnancy and your health. Do not use a generic online stopping schedule: ask your prescribing clinician for an individual plan. If you become pregnant while taking a medicine you are concerned about, contact your rheumatology or maternity team promptly rather than making an unsupervised change.

Symptoms during pregnancy

Some people experience changes in arthritis symptoms during pregnancy or after delivery. Keep a record of pain, swelling, fatigue and function, and report significant changes to your care team. Gentle physical activity may help, but the right approach depends on pregnancy symptoms and medical advice.

Planning for birth and the postnatal period

Ask your team about flare management, breastfeeding-compatible medicines and practical support after delivery. Postnatal symptoms and treatment needs can change, so arrange follow-up in advance.

When to get urgent help

Seek urgent maternity assessment for concerning pregnancy symptoms such as vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, severe headache with visual symptoms, or reduced fetal movements once you have started to notice a regular movement pattern. For sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness or collapse, seek emergency help.
